questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has a year of tiredness, bloating that is worse after bread or pasta, and intermittent loose stools. She has lost 3 kg. Her nails have become spoon-shaped and she looks pale. She does not drink alcohol and has normal periods. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bloating after bread or pasta, loose stools, weight loss and iron deficiency (koilonychia, pallor, low ferritin) is coeliac disease: villous atrophy causes malabsorption.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Gluten-related bloating + iron deficiency with normal periods = coeliac.

elim: Usually right iliac fossa pain, raised inflammatory markers and sometimes blood or perianal disease.
Does not cause iron deficiency anaemia, koilonychia or weight loss.
Symptoms follow dairy, not bread or pasta, and there is no anaemia.
Her periods are normal, and this would not explain bloating after gluten.

steps.x: A: Coeliac disease. Unexplained iron deficiency: think coeliac.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has 8 months of loose, pale, bulky stools that smell offensive and float, needing several flushes. He has lost 6 kg and has occasional nausea. He drinks 4 units of alcohol a week and has no abdominal pain. His sister has type 1 diabetes. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic non-bloody diarrhoea with steatorrhoea (pale, offensive, bulky stools), weight loss and low folate in a man with an autoimmune family history is coeliac disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: pale, bulky stools that smell offensive and float
steps.x: Steatorrhoea without pain or alcohol excess, plus autoimmune family history = coeliac.

elim: Watery diarrhoea after ileal resection or cholecystectomy, not with folate deficiency and a family history of autoimmunity.
Steatorrhoea with epigastric pain in heavy drinkers; his alcohol intake is low.
Possible, but chronic symptoms with low folate and autoimmune family history favour coeliac.
Bloody diarrhoea with urgency, not steatorrhoea.

steps.x: C: Coeliac disease. Coeliac: chronic non-bloody diarrhoea and steatorrhoea.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has 6 months of aching bones and difficulty climbing stairs and getting out of chairs. She has had loose stools for years, which she put down to a 'sensitive stomach'. She rarely goes outside without sunscreen. Proximal leg power is 4/5.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Bone pain, proximal myopathy, low calcium and phosphate with high ALP and low vitamin D is osteomalacia. With long-standing loose stools the cause is coeliac disease, from malabsorption of calcium and vitamin D.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
Osteomalacia + chronic diarrhoea = malabsorption, coeliac.

elim: Her creatinine would be raised and phosphate high, not low.
Causes high calcium with lytic lesions, not low calcium and phosphate.
Shoulder and hip girdle stiffness in over-50s with a raised ESR; bone profile normal.
Causes high calcium.

steps.x: B: Coeliac disease. Coeliac disease can present with osteomalacia.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has had an intensely itchy rash on her buttocks, lower back and the backs of her forearms for 4 months. There are clusters of tiny blisters and many excoriated papules. Topical steroids have not helped. She has occasional bloating and loose stools. Skin biopsy shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.e: Grouped itchy papulovesicles on extensor surfaces and buttocks with granular IgA in the dermal papillae is dermatitis herpetiformis, the classic and specific skin manifestation of coeliac disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying condition?

clues: granular IgA in the dermal papillae
steps.x: Dermatitis herpetiformis means coeliac disease.

elim: Flexural, dry and lichenified skin, not grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces.
Large tense blisters in older people with linear IgG and C3.
Silvery plaques without vesicles or IgA deposits.
Burrows in finger webs and itching in contacts; no IgA on biopsy.

steps.x: C: Coeliac disease. DH is the classic cutaneous sign of coeliac disease.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman was diagnosed with coeliac disease on duodenal biopsy last month. Her GP reviews her and explains that some other conditions are more common in people with coeliac disease, so new symptoms such as thirst, weight loss or palpitations should be reported.
questions.q: Which condition is most strongly associated with coeliac disease?
questions.e: Coeliac disease is associated with other autoimmune conditions, especially type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease (including Graves').

steps.x: The question asks: Which condition is most strongly associated with coeliac disease?
Coeliac clusters with type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease.

elim: Not linked with coeliac disease.
Not autoimmune.
A genetic iron overload disorder, not associated.
Not a recognised association.

steps.x: E: Type 1 diabetes. Associations: type 1 diabetes, Graves'/autoimmune thyroid disease.

questions.stem: A 20 month old girl has had loose, foul-smelling stools and irritability since she started eating cereals and bread at 8 months. She has dropped from the 50th to the 9th centile for weight. Her father has coeliac disease. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 90/55 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Her abdomen is distended and her buttocks are wasted.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Faltering growth, abdominal distension, wasted buttocks and loose stools beginning after gluten was introduced, with a family history, is coeliac disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: since she started eating cereals and bread
dropped from the 50th to the 9th centile
steps.x: Symptoms after weaning onto gluten + faltering growth = coeliac.

elim: Usually starts with formula or milk before cereals.
Recurrent chest infections and meconium ileus; symptoms would precede weaning.
Constipation and delayed meconium, not loose stools.
Undigested food in stools with normal growth.

steps.x: A: Coeliac disease. Family history is a key risk factor.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with coeliac disease diagnosed 15 years ago admits she eats bread most days. She fell from standing onto her outstretched hand and fractured her distal radius. She has never taken steroids and has regular periods. A DEXA scan is arranged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on DEXA scan?
questions.e: A fragility fracture in a premenopausal woman with poorly controlled coeliac disease suggests osteoporosis (T-score -2.5 or lower) from malabsorption. Poor adherence to the gluten-free diet raises the risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on DEXA scan?
Poorly controlled coeliac + fragility fracture = osteoporosis.

elim: Suggest metastases (for example prostate), not malabsorption.
Coeliac disease with poor adherence reduces bone mineral density.
Diagnosed on X-ray and bone scan with a raised ALP, not DEXA.
Seen in osteopetrosis or sclerotic metastases.

steps.x: C: Osteoporosis. Coeliac reduces bone mineral density.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with coeliac disease has 3 months of weight loss, fevers and abdominal pain despite a strict gluten-free diet. He is admitted with peritonitis from a jejunal perforation. Histology of the resected jejunum shows sheets of atypical T lymphocytes infiltrating the bowel wall.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Coeliac disease increases the risk of small bowel lymphoma and adenocarcinoma, especially enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL), a non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can perforate the small bowel.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Coeliac + T-cell small bowel lymphoma = EATL.

elim: A B-cell lymphoma with a 'starry sky' pattern, linked to EBV.
A B-cell lymphoma, not T-cell.
B-cell lymphoma of the stomach linked to H. pylori.
Also more common in coeliac disease, but histology shows lymphocytes, not glands.

steps.x: C: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma. EATL is the key coeliac malignancy.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with newly diagnosed coeliac disease has tiredness and breathlessness on exertion. Her iron, folate and B12 stores are all low because of malabsorption. Her doctor expects the full blood count to reflect the mixed deficiency.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her full blood count?
questions.e: Mixed iron (microcytic) and folate/B12 (macrocytic) deficiency can give a normal, high or low MCV with a high RDW, showing two red cell populations.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on her full blood count?

clues: iron, folate and B12 stores are all low
steps.x: Two deficiencies pulling the MCV opposite ways = normal MCV, high RDW.

elim: Uniform macrocytes suggest a single B12 or folate deficiency.
Seen in thalassaemia trait.
Pancytopenia is not typical.
Polycythaemia is not a feature.

steps.x: D: Normal MCV with high RDW. Coeliac anaemia: variable MCV, high RDW.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man is admitted with 3 weeks of profuse watery diarrhoea up to 12 times a day, 9 kg weight loss and dizziness on standing. He has had bloating for years. There is no blood in the stool and no travel. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Stool cultures are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe diarrhoea and weight loss should raise concern for coeliac disease and prompt urgent assessment. A strongly positive anti-tTG with normal total IgA supports the diagnosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Severe malabsorptive diarrhoea + strongly positive tTG = coeliac.

elim: Cultures are negative and symptoms are on a background of years of bloating.
Does not cause severe weight loss, hypokalaemia and low albumin.
Would cause weight loss but not a strongly positive anti-tTG.
Bloody diarrhoea with urgency.

steps.x: A: Coeliac disease. Severe diarrhoea and weight loss: urgent assessment for coeliac.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman's younger brother was diagnosed with coeliac disease last year. She has had mild tiredness and occasional bloating for 2 years but no diarrhoea. Her haemoglobin is 112 g/L with a ferritin of 9 µg/L. Her periods are light. Anti-tTG IgA is 64 U/mL (<7) with normal total IgA.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A first-degree relative with coeliac disease, iron deficiency without blood loss and a positive anti-tTG point to coeliac disease, which can be minimally symptomatic.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: younger brother was diagnosed with coeliac disease
steps.x: Family history + iron deficiency + positive tTG = coeliac.

elim: Ferritin would be normal or high.
Does not cause iron deficiency or positive anti-tTG.
Her periods are light.
Serology is negative in gluten sensitivity.

steps.x: B: Coeliac disease. Family history is a risk factor; symptoms can be subtle.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man is referred by his GP with fatigue, intermittent loose stools and bloating after meals for 18 months. His anti-tTG IgA is strongly positive and his ferritin is very low. The registrar examines him carefully in clinic before arranging gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Malabsorption of iron in coeliac disease causes iron deficiency anaemia, giving pallor and koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
Iron deficiency signs: pallor and spoon nails.

elim: Features of chronic liver disease.
Associated with inflammatory bowel disease and sarcoidosis.
Suggests Crohn's disease.
Hyperlipidaemia.

steps.x: C: Koilonychia and conjunctival pallor. Coeliac exam: koilonychia, pallor.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man with biopsy-confirmed coeliac disease was well for a year on a gluten-free diet. Over 3 months his bloating and loose stools have returned. He started a new job and eats lunch from a sandwich shop, choosing 'healthy' wholegrain and barley salads. His anti-tTG has risen from 4 to 58 U/mL (<7).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.e: A rising anti-tTG with returning symptoms means ongoing gluten exposure (barley contains gluten; sandwich shop food is often contaminated). Monitoring tTG and symptoms detects poor adherence, which also raises the risk of complications.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
tTG back up = gluten back in.

elim: Possible in refractory disease, but a rising tTG with a clear gluten source points to dietary exposure.
Does not raise the anti-tTG.
Would not raise the anti-tTG.
Does not explain the rising anti-tTG.

steps.x: D: Ongoing gluten ingestion. tTG levels monitor adherence.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman develops bloating and loose stools whenever she eats bread. She has no hives, wheeze or lip swelling after eating. Her anti-tTG IgA is 85 U/mL (<7) and duodenal biopsies show intra-epithelial lymphocytes, crypt hyperplasia and sub-total villous atrophy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A T-cell-mediated autoimmune reaction to gluten causing villous atrophy, with positive anti-tTG and the classic histology, is coeliac disease. Gluten sensitivity has normal serology and histology.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: no hives, wheeze or lip swelling
steps.x: Positive tTG + villous atrophy = coeliac, not sensitivity or allergy.

elim: Biopsies would be normal and serology negative.
Symptoms with gluten but negative serology and normal histology.
Similar histology but follows prolonged residence in the tropics, with negative tTG.
An IgE-mediated reaction with hives, wheeze or anaphylaxis within minutes.

steps.x: A: Coeliac disease. Coeliac: T-cell-mediated, villous atrophy.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has 6 months of bloating and loose stools. He eats a normal diet including bread daily. Investigations: total IgA 2.0 g/L (0.7–4.0), anti-tTG IgA 72 U/mL (<7), ferritin 11 µg/L (15–300). He has not changed his diet since the blood test.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Positive serology is followed by OGD with duodenal (or jejunal) biopsy while still eating gluten: the gold standard for diagnosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
Positive serology on gluten = biopsy to confirm.

elim: Supports the diagnosis but does not confirm it; histology does.
Not the standard first diagnostic test.
Coeliac disease affects the small bowel, not the colon.
Has a high negative predictive value but cannot confirm disease.

steps.x: D: Gastroscopy with duodenal biopsy. Gold standard: OGD with duodenal biopsy.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman with a positive anti-tTG IgA is undergoing gastroscopy. The oesophagus and stomach look normal. The endoscopist takes biopsies from the second part of the duodenum and describes its appearance in the report, which will be compared with the histology later.
questions.q: Which is the most likely endoscopic finding in the duodenum?
o: Cobblestone mucosa with deep fissuring ulcers
Flattened mucosa with scalloping of the folds
Single deep ulcer with a visible vessel
questions.e: In coeliac disease the duodenal mucosa looks flattened, with scalloping and loss of the folds, reflecting villous atrophy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely endoscopic finding in the duodenum?
Endoscopic coeliac: scalloped, flattened duodenum.

elim: Crohn's disease.
Candida, usually in the oesophagus.
Possible in mild disease, but the typical finding is loss of folds.
Peptic ulcer disease.

steps.x: B: Flattened mucosa with scalloping of the folds. Flattened duodenal mucosa, scalloped folds.

questions.stem: A 14 year old boy is diagnosed with type 1 diabetes after presenting with thirst and weight loss. He has no gastrointestinal symptoms. His mother asks whether he needs any other tests. The paediatric diabetes team follows NICE guidance for a new diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation for coeliac disease?
questions.e: NICE recommends testing for coeliac disease in every new diagnosis of type 1 diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease, even without symptoms. First-line testing is total IgA with IgA anti-tTG.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation for coeliac disease?

clues: NICE guidance for a new diagnosis
steps.x: New T1DM or autoimmune thyroid disease = test for coeliac.

elim: Not a screening test; reserved for positive serology.
A marker of bowel inflammation, not coeliac disease.
Not the first-line test.
NICE recommends testing all new diagnoses of type 1 diabetes.

steps.x: E: Total IgA and IgA anti-tTG. NICE: test for coeliac in new T1DM or autoimmune thyroid disease.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man has 9 months of intermittent bloating, abdominal discomfort and loose stools with no blood. He has been told he probably has irritable bowel syndrome. He eats bread and pasta daily. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. His abdomen is soft and non-tender.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Coeliac serology (total IgA with IgA anti-tTG) is the first-line test and should be done before labelling anyone with IBS, while they are eating gluten.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
Before diagnosing IBS, exclude coeliac with serology.

elim: Not first-line for young patients with no red flags.
Not indicated without red flags.
Done after positive serology, not first.
For lactose intolerance or bacterial overgrowth.

steps.x: E: Total IgA and IgA anti-tTG. First-line: total IgA and IgA anti-tTG.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has chronic loose stools, weight loss and iron deficiency. She eats gluten daily. Her IgA anti-tTG is 1 U/mL (<7). Her total IgA is undetectable at <0.07 g/L (0.7–4.0). She has had recurrent sinus infections.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her anti-tTG result?
o: Selective IgA deficiency causing a false negative
questions.e: IgA deficiency (in about 2% of coeliac patients) gives a false negative IgA anti-tTG. The second-line test is IgG anti-tTG (or IgG EMA/DGP).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for her anti-tTG result?
Always check total IgA: no IgA means a false negative.

elim: A negative IgA test is unreliable when total IgA is absent.
The total IgA explains the result.
She eats gluten daily.
Does not suppress anti-tTG.

steps.x: E: Selective IgA deficiency causing a false negative. IgA deficient: use IgG anti-tTG.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman cut gluten out of her diet a year ago after reading about it and her bloating improved. Her GP wants to find out whether she has coeliac disease, as her mother does. Her anti-tTG IgA today is 3 U/mL (<7) with normal total IgA.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Eat gluten daily for at least 6 weeks, then repeat serology
Eat gluten for 3 days, then repeat serology
Reassure that coeliac disease is excluded
questions.e: Serology and histology normalise without gluten. Gluten must be reintroduced (in more than one meal a day) for at least 6 weeks before serological testing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step?

clues: cut gluten out of her diet a year ago
steps.x: Negative tTG on a gluten-free diet means nothing: rechallenge first.

elim: Coeliac disease has not been excluded while she avoids gluten.
Too short to produce antibodies.
Histology will also recover on a gluten-free diet.
A negative test on a gluten-free diet is unreliable.

steps.x: B: Eat gluten daily for at least 6 weeks, then repeat serology. Gluten challenge for at least 6 weeks before testing.

questions.stem: A 52 year old postmenopausal woman has just been diagnosed with coeliac disease after years of loose stools. Her calcium and vitamin D are slightly low. She has never had a fracture. Her gastroenterologist wants to assess the long-term effect of malabsorption on her skeleton.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine
questions.e: A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density to assess osteoporosis risk in coeliac disease, especially with malabsorption or postmenopausal status.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: calcium and vitamin D are slightly low
effect of malabsorption on her skeleton
steps.x: Bone density in coeliac = DEXA.

elim: For metastases or Paget's disease.
Insensitive for bone loss.
Does not measure bone density.
Does not assess bone density.

steps.x: B: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA). DEXA for bone density in coeliac disease.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man was diagnosed with coeliac disease 6 months ago and says he is following a strict gluten-free diet. His symptoms have improved. His annual review is due and the dietitian wants an objective marker of adherence.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Anti-tTG levels fall on a gluten-free diet and rise with gluten exposure, so they are used with symptoms to monitor adherence.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
Monitor adherence with tTG.

elim: Tests pancreatic function.
Genetic; never changes.
Not routine; reserved for persisting symptoms.
Recovers slowly and is not specific to gluten exposure.

steps.x: A: Anti-tTG antibody level. Monitor with tTG levels and symptoms.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with loose stools and iron deficiency has an IgA anti-tTG of 15 U/mL (<7), only modestly raised. Her total IgA is normal. Her gastroenterologist wants a second, highly specific antibody test to support the diagnosis before endoscopy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional antibody test?
questions.e: Raised anti-endomysial antibodies (EMA), along with positive tTG, support the diagnosis of coeliac disease and are highly specific.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate additional antibody test?
Second coeliac antibody = EMA.

elim: For primary biliary cholangitis.
For vasculitis.
For autoimmune hepatitis.
For rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: A: Anti-endomysial antibodies. EMA supports the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman has just been diagnosed with coeliac disease on duodenal biopsy. She is seeing the dietitian and wants to plan meals for the week. She lists foods she usually eats at home and at work and asks which are safe to keep in her diet.
questions.q: Which food can she eat safely?
questions.e: Rice, potatoes and corn (maize) are naturally gluten-free. Wheat (including couscous and pasta), barley and rye contain gluten.

steps.x: The question asks: Which food can she eat safely?
Avoid wheat, barley and rye; rice, potato and corn are safe.

elim: Barley contains gluten.
Made from wheat.
Rye contains gluten.
Made from wheat.

steps.x: C: Jacket potato. Gluten-free staples: rice, potatoes, corn.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has coeliac disease confirmed on duodenal biopsy. He has tiredness and iron deficiency anaemia. Investigations: haemoglobin 104 g/L (130–180), ferritin 7 µg/L (15–300). His B12 and folate are normal. He wants to know what treatment he needs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Gluten-free diet until symptoms settle, then reintroduce gluten
questions.e: The only definitive treatment is lifelong strict exclusion of gluten, with nutritional support (iron and vitamins) as needed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Lifelong gluten-free diet + replace what is missing.

elim: The diet is lifelong.
Treats the anaemia but not the cause.
Not first-line; reserved for refractory disease.
Even small amounts cause damage; exclusion must be strict.

steps.x: A: Gluten-free diet and oral iron. Strict lifelong gluten-free diet plus iron.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has newly diagnosed dermatitis herpetiformis confirmed on skin biopsy, with positive coeliac serology. The itch is keeping her awake. She has normal G6PD levels. She has not yet changed her diet and asks for something that will work quickly.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Dapsone and a strict gluten-free diet
questions.e: Dermatitis herpetiformis is treated with dapsone for rapid relief plus a strict gluten-free diet, which treats the cause and lets dapsone be reduced.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
DH: dapsone now, gluten-free diet for life.

Do not control dermatitis herpetiformis.
Of limited benefit.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with coeliac disease has a blood film showing Howell-Jolly bodies. She had a pneumococcal vaccine at diagnosis 5 years ago and is up to date with her annual influenza vaccine. She asks whether any more vaccines are needed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
questions.e: Hyposplenism in coeliac disease raises the risk of encapsulated bacteria, so pneumococcal vaccine is given every 5 years. Hers is now due.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice?
Coeliac hyposplenism: pneumococcal vaccine every 5 years.

elim: Not indicated.
Not routine in coeliac hyposplenism.
Hyposplenism needs repeated protection.
Given every 5 years, not yearly.

steps.x: A: A pneumococcal booster now. 5-yearly pneumococcal vaccine.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with coeliac disease, well controlled on a gluten-free diet, has a positive pregnancy test. She is 6 weeks pregnant and started over-the-counter folic acid 400 micrograms daily when the test was positive. She takes no other medicines. Her BMI is 23.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue folic acid 400 micrograms until 12 weeks
Folic acid 5 mg daily throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding
Folic acid 5 mg daily until 12 weeks
Stop folic acid as she is past 4 weeks
questions.e: Pregnant women with coeliac disease need folic acid 5 mg daily until 12 weeks, because of reduced folate absorption.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Coeliac + pregnancy = high-dose folic acid.

elim: Malabsorption means a higher dose is needed.
The high dose is given until 12 weeks.
Supplementation continues until 12 weeks.
Not indicated.

steps.x: C: Folic acid 5 mg daily until 12 weeks. 5 mg folic acid until 12 weeks.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has had coeliac disease for 3 years and feels well on a gluten-free diet. His GP asks what long-term follow-up the practice should organise for him, as he has not been seen since his diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term follow-up?
o: Annual review of symptoms, diet, weight, bloods and anti-tTG
questions.e: Coeliac disease needs regular (usually annual) review: symptoms, adherence, weight, bloods for malabsorption and anti-tTG, with surveillance for osteoporosis and lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman sees her GP with 4 weeks of up to 10 loose stools a day and 7 kg weight loss. She feels lightheaded. She has had bloating for years. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 94/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. A blood test 2 years ago showed iron deficiency that was never explained.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Advise a gluten-free diet now and review in 6 months
Prescribe loperamide and review in 4 weeks
Stool culture and review in 2 weeks
questions.e: Severe diarrhoea and weight loss, especially with a background suggesting coeliac disease, prompt urgent assessment, with fluids, electrolytes and coeliac serology taken while she still eats gluten.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: iron deficiency that was never explained
steps.x: Dehydration and rapid weight loss = urgent assessment.

elim: Removing gluten before testing makes diagnosis impossible.
Delays assessment of a significant illness.
Too slow with dehydration and rapid weight loss.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has newly diagnosed coeliac disease. Investigations: haemoglobin 108 g/L (130–180), MCV 106 fL (80–100), serum B12 120 ng/L (>200), folate 2.0 µg/L (3–20), ferritin 80 µg/L (15–300). He has started a gluten-free diet. He has no neurological symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
o: No supplements, as the diet will correct it
Replace vitamin B12 and folic acid
questions.e: Malabsorption of B12 and folate gives a macrocytic anaemia. Nutritional support replaces both, starting B12 before or with folate.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
Macrocytosis with low B12 and folate = replace both.

His ferritin is normal.

steps.x: E: Replace vitamin B12 and folic acid. Nutritional support: vitamins and iron as needed.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman with coeliac disease has a DEXA scan showing a T-score of -2.7 at the lumbar spine. She has no fractures. She follows a strict gluten-free diet. Her calcium intake is low and her 25-OH vitamin D is 28 nmol/L (>50). Her renal function is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Calcium and vitamin D, then a bisphosphonate
No treatment, as the gluten-free diet will correct it
questions.e: Coeliac disease reduces bone mineral density. Replace vitamin D and calcium first, then start a bisphosphonate for osteoporosis, with continued surveillance.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Osteoporosis + low vitamin D: replete first, then bisphosphonate.

elim: Not used for osteoporosis in this setting.
Does not correct her vitamin D deficiency.
Osteoporosis needs active treatment.
No primary hyperparathyroidism.

steps.x: B: Calcium and vitamin D, then a bisphosphonate. Surveillance and treatment of osteoporosis in coeliac disease.

questions.stem: A scientist explains to medical students how gluten triggers coeliac disease. A component of wheat gluten crosses the damaged epithelium and is chemically modified in the lamina propria by an enzyme, which makes it bind more tightly to HLA molecules and greatly increases its immunogenicity.
questions.q: Which enzyme modifies the gluten peptide?
questions.e: Gliadin is deamidated by tissue transglutaminase, increasing its immunogenicity. Antibodies against tTG are the basis of the serology test.

steps.x: The question asks: Which enzyme modifies the gluten peptide?
Deamidation of gliadin = tissue transglutaminase.

elim: Activates trypsinogen in the duodenum.
Digests lactose.
A gastric protease; does not deamidate gliadin.
A pancreatic protease.

steps.x: D: Tissue transglutaminase. tTG deamidates gliadin.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man with coeliac disease asks why his small bowel is damaged by bread when his flatmate eats it without problems. His consultant explains that gliadin peptides are presented by particular HLA class II molecules to immune cells in the lamina propria.
questions.q: Which is the main immune mechanism causing the mucosal damage?
o: Gliadin-specific CD4 T-cell response restricted by HLA-DQ2/DQ8
Immune complex deposition in vessel walls
questions.e: Coeliac disease is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune condition: in genetically susceptible people (HLA-DQ2/DQ8), CD4 T cells respond to deamidated gliadin, driving an inflammatory cascade.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the main immune mechanism causing the mucosal damage?
HLA class II + T cells = HLA-DQ2/DQ8-restricted T-cell response.

elim: IgE causes type I allergy, as in wheat allergy.
Type III hypersensitivity, as in vasculitis.
Type I hypersensitivity.
Describes infective colitis.

steps.x: B: Gliadin-specific CD4 T-cell response restricted by HLA-DQ2/DQ8. T-cell-mediated response in HLA-DQ2/DQ8 carriers.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman with untreated coeliac disease has iron deficiency anaemia despite eating red meat and leafy greens. Her duodenal biopsy shows sub-total villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia. A student on the ward round asks why the iron in her food is not being absorbed.
questions.q: Which best explains her iron deficiency?
o: Loss of absorptive surface in the duodenum
questions.e: Iron is absorbed in the duodenum. Inflammation causes villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia, dramatically reducing absorptive surface area, so iron, folate, B12, calcium and fat-soluble vitamins are malabsorbed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains her iron deficiency?
Villi gone in the duodenum = iron not absorbed.

elim: Pernicious anaemia, causing B12 deficiency.
Not the mechanism.
Coeliac disease does not cause significant blood loss.
Iron is absorbed in the duodenum, not the colon.

steps.x: D: Loss of absorptive surface in the duodenum. Villous atrophy reduces absorptive surface.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man with undiagnosed coeliac disease and steatorrhoea bruises easily and bled for a long time after a tooth extraction. Investigations: PT 21 s (10–13), APTT 38 s (25–35), platelets 260 ×10⁹/L (150–400). His liver tests are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his bleeding tendency?
questions.e: Fat malabsorption causes steatorrhoea and deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Low vitamin K reduces factors II, VII, IX and X, prolonging the PT.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his bleeding tendency?
Steatorrhoea + long PT = vitamin K malabsorption.

elim: His platelets are normal.
Would prolong the APTT much more than the PT.
Liver tests are normal.
Normal PT; prolonged bleeding time.

steps.x: D: Malabsorption of vitamin K. Fat malabsorption: fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with long-standing coeliac disease is admitted with pneumococcal septicaemia. Her blood film shows Howell-Jolly bodies and target cells. She has never had abdominal surgery and has not had a pneumococcal vaccine. Ultrasound shows a small spleen.
questions.q: Which best explains her susceptibility to this infection?
o: IgA deficiency causing loss of mucosal immunity
Reduced splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria
questions.e: Coeliac disease causes hyposplenism through an unclear autoimmune mechanism. The spleen clears encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus, hence 5-yearly pneumococcal vaccination.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains her susceptibility to this infection?
Howell-Jolly bodies = hyposplenism = encapsulated organisms.

elim: Not a feature of coeliac disease.
Present in a few, but does not explain Howell-Jolly bodies.
Not the main mechanism.
Not typical of coeliac disease.

steps.x: D: Reduced splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria. Hyposplenism: susceptibility to encapsulated organisms.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has an itchy blistering rash on his elbows and buttocks. Perilesional skin biopsy shows granular deposits in the dermal papillae on direct immunofluorescence. After a year on a strict gluten-free diet the rash has cleared and he no longer needs dapsone.
questions.q: Which best explains the rash and why it cleared?
o: IgA immune complex deposition driven by gluten
IgE-mediated mast cell release triggered by wheat
questions.e: Dermatitis herpetiformis results from IgA immune complex deposition in the dermis, triggered by the same gluten-driven immune process as the gut disease, so it responds to a gluten-free diet.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains the rash and why it cleared?

clues: granular deposits in the dermal papillae
strict gluten-free diet the rash has cleared
steps.x: Granular IgA in papillae, cured by removing gluten = DH.

elim: Wheat allergy gives urticaria, not IgA deposits.
Pemphigus vulgaris.
Bullous pemphigoid.
Polymorphic light eruption.

steps.x: A: IgA immune complex deposition driven by gluten. DH: IgA deposits, gluten-driven.

questions.stem: A medical student asks a gastroenterologist why a patient who has ignored his gluten-free diet for 20 years is at much higher risk of small bowel lymphoma than a patient who has followed it strictly since diagnosis. Both were diagnosed in their twenties.
questions.q: Which best explains the increased lymphoma risk?
o: Chronic Epstein-Barr virus infection of B cells
Direct carcinogenic effect of gluten on enterocytes
Lifelong T-cell-driven inflammation causing malignant transformation
questions.e: Poorly controlled coeliac disease creates a lifelong T-cell-driven inflammatory state that increases the risk of malignant transformation, particularly enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains the increased lymphoma risk?

clues: ignored his gluten-free diet for 20 years
steps.x: Ongoing T-cell inflammation = T-cell lymphoma risk.

elim: Linked to Burkitt and Hodgkin lymphoma, not EATL.
Gluten is not a carcinogen.
Linked to gastric MALT lymphoma.
Not a recognised cause.

steps.x: D: Lifelong T-cell-driven inflammation causing malignant transformation. Chronic T-cell inflammation drives EATL.
